name: Focal length
seoTitle: Focal length Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Focal length: work out magnification from the object size and the image size. A free other calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Focal length calculator turns the object size, the image size and the object distance into magnification. It is built for whatever you happen to be working on. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Focal length calculator work?
sections.html:
The Focal length calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports magnification in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the object size, the image size and the object distance.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in centimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in millimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Focal length calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Magnification=image size ÷ object size
Focal length=1000 × magnification × object distance ÷ (magnification + 1)
Focal length=(1 ÷ 2) × image size ÷ ((magnification + 1) × the tangent of ((1 ÷ 360) × PI × angle of view))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Object size = 30 cm and Image size = 30 mm. Working through the relationship above gives Magnification = 1.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Magnification = 1 should be roughly the size you expected from Object size = 30 cm and Image size = 30 mm.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.
  • Shown in millimeters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.
  • Shown in degrees, and convertible to any of the 12 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Angle, opening in degrees

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Focal length calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the object size, the image size and the object distance — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Focal length calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns magnification, derived from the object size, the image size and the object distance. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Focal length calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the object size, the image size and the object distance, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter object size in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Object size opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Magnification = 1. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Focal length calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
